SK2030 Detect NaN with IsNaN rather than equality

A floating-point value is compared with == or != against a constant NaN, which is the one comparison guaranteed never to answer the question it was written to ask.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since1.3
SupersedesS2688

Why

NaN is unordered with everything including itself, so x == double.NaN is false even when x is NaN and x != double.NaN is true even when it is. The check written to catch the bad case is the shape that cannot catch it. double.IsNaN is the operation that was meant, and the rewrite is mechanical.

Example

Instead of:

if (result == double.NaN) { Report(); }

Write:

if (double.IsNaN(result)) { Report(); }

When it does not fire

Only == and != between two floating-point operands are examined, and exactly one side must be a compile-time constant NaN: double.NaN, float.NaN, a const initialized from one, or a constant expression that folds to NaN. != is reported alongside == because it is always true rather than always false; it carries its own message and a negated fix. NaN reached through a non-constant field, property, method result or parameter is one indirection the rule does not follow, because a static readonly double is not decidable from the comparison alone. Lifted comparisons on nullable operands, user-defined equality operators, operands whose own type is not float or double before conversion, and comparisons with NaN on both sides are excluded; the last names no operand to test. Relational comparisons with NaN are also constant and are deliberately not reported, because the rewrite is not a single IsNaN call. SK2003 excludes NaN sentinels, so the two rules do not overlap.

Configuration
